chunks: Why servos are so precise. The question: How are servo motors so precise in their movement?
A servo is precise because it never trusts the motor. It measures where the shaft really is, compares that with the command, and keeps correcting until the error is nearly zero.
So the precision comes from the sensor and the loop, not from how well the motor behaves.
Be careful about one word, though: resolution (the sensor's smallest step) is not the same as accuracy (being at the true position).
Think of cruise control in a car. Without it, a hill slows you down and you end up wherever the road takes you.
With it, the car measures its speed, sees the drop, and adds throttle until the speed matches the setting.
The analogy also shows the catch: if the speedometer itself reads wrong, cruise control holds the wrong speed very precisely.
Each extra bit halves the step.
Beyond about 17–20 bits, extra resolution mostly shows sensor noise and mechanical imperfection rather than real position information, which is why you also see accuracy specified in arc-seconds.
Encoder: a sensor that reports the shaft angle as a count. Resolution: the smallest position step the sensor can report. Accuracy: how close the position is to the true one.
Stiffness: how little the shaft moves when a load pushes on it. A loop that pushes harder for each bit of error is stiffer.
Integral term: a control part that keeps increasing the drive until the steady error reaches zero. Backlash: the free play between meshing gears.
A 17-bit encoder splits one turn into 2 to the 17 equals 131 072 counts, so each count is about 0. 0027 degrees.
Put it on the motor behind a 10:1 gearbox, and the output steps are ten times finer, about 0. 00027 degrees. Now give the gearbox 0.
5 degrees of backlash and hang a 100 mm arm on it. That slop lets the arm tip wander about 0. 87 mm, and the encoder on the motor cannot even see it.
That is the whole idea: feedback gives the precision, and the mechanics limit it.
